title: Keep him whole
hookLine: Rumi was a Muslim steeped in the Qur'an, and popular versions often strip that out; we won't
carry: a love he thought was wide

cards: In English, Rumi's lines turn up on wedding invitations, yoga studio walls and endless social posts. They're lovely. And some of them have had something quietly taken out.

In some popular English versions, the mentions of God, of the Prophet, of the Qur'an, of the prayer he prayed five times a day, have been softened or dropped. What's left sounds like a poet from nowhere.
But he was from somewhere. This week you've walked his road. Today's word is the name for the kind of Muslim he was: Sufi.

teach.b: A Sufi is someone on the inward, mystical path within Islam.
The usual explanation is that the word comes from suf, Arabic for wool, for the rough wool robes some early ascetics wore. Others have proposed different roots, and nobody can settle it.
Sufis aim to know God not only through law and learning, but through love, remembrance and the discipline of the heart.
They pray the same prayers and keep the same fast as other Muslims; they add practices of remembrance, poetry and music, and they gather around teachers. Now put Rumi back together.
The boy who walked west was the son of a Muslim preacher.
The scholar of Konya taught Islamic law. The friend who arrived tested him with a question about the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him.
And the Masnavi is so thick with verses of the Qur'an that tradition credits a later Persian poet, Jami, with calling it the Qur'an in the Persian tongue.
When the reed flute you'll meet next week cries to go home, some readers hear a verse Muslims say at a loss. In Pickthall's translation: "Lo! we are Allah's and lo! unto Him we are returning."
That's the ground his poems grow from. People from other paths, and none, love Rumi, and that's welcome here; he wrote about a love he thought was wide. But loving him well means meeting him whole.
So in this camp, when he names God, the Prophet or a verse, i'll say so.

how: Sufi Muslims keep the daily prayers and the fast of Ramadan like other Muslims, and add practices of remembrance of God (dhikr), poetry and sometimes music, often in circles gathered around a teacher.

o: one on the inward, mystical path within Islam
a Hindu priest who tends a temple
a wandering beggar monk outside any religion

games.q: what goes with what — tap the pairs.

s: Rumi was a poet with no religion
he was a Muslim scholar and a Sufi, and his poems are threaded with the Qur'an.

games.q: you're putting a Rumi line on a card for a friend. the original names God and a verse of the Qur'an. what do you do?
o: drop the religious part so it fits everyone.
keep it whole, and say where it comes from.
swap in a different poet's line.
games.why: this path keeps him whole: when he names God, the Prophet or a verse, we say so. anyone can love the poem; it just comes from somewhere.

practice: The verse you just heard is what Muslims traditionally say when they hear of a death, or any loss: we belong to God, and to God we return.
Hold that sentence for a minute without deciding what you think of it, just knowing that someone, somewhere, will say it today.
Then look back over the week: the road west, the respectable one, someone arrives, the grief sang, the long book.

wordCard.voice: Sufi. One who walks the inward, mystical path within Islam, most likely named for the rough wool robes of early ascetics. Rumi was one. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian and Arabic: Sufi, most often traced to suf, wool.
